source.title: Recontextualization Mitigates Specification Gaming Without Modifying the Specification

record.file_problem: The post text is present in full, but most plotted results are not included as readable values; some equations and table content are also missing or flattened.
record.tranche_reason: The study tests whether RL and other post-training procedures can produce misbehavior, and whether prompt recontextualization reduces it, using different tasks and measures from the original claim.
record.gate_note: The study reports outcomes for specification gaming, test-case hacking, deception, and sycophancy, including evaluations under neutral prompts. Rows below cover those reported results. Results cited from other work, coherence and instruction-following metrics, and plots without an explicit outcome relevant to the claim are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study measures whether recontextualization reduces the target misbehavior that a misspecified training signal rewards. That misbehavior is evaluation hacking, test-case hacking, deception or sycophancy, and it is measured on held-out data from the same task. No result measures broad misaligned answers on unrelated free-form questions. So the rows do not bear on emergent misalignment (V4) or on preventing it (V6). Recontextualization is related to inoculation prompting, but here it targets in-distribution specification gaming, a different construct.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors add that with a strong (95%) lie detector, standard training reduces deception more than recontextualization (4.4 vs 6.0). Recontextualization also costs some instruction following (IFEval drops of about 2%).
record.recipe_differences: The post studies prompt recontextualization in reward-based training, including GRPO, Expert Iteration, and Best-of-N followed by SFT. It does not reproduce the original narrow insecure-code fine-tune and unrelated-prompt evaluation.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcomes depend on the contrast between data-generation and training prompts, the specific prompt wording, lie-detector recall, and inference instructions. For GRPO, the authors report that the importance-ratio implementation and resulting regularization affected outcomes.

fits_no_version.finding: Training on misspecified signals (SFT on Best-of-N selections, GRPO with a weak lie detector, Expert Iteration rewarding sycophancy) increases the rewarded misbehavior on held-out same-task data. A 95%-recall detector instead reduces deception (11.2 to 4.4).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Misspecified training rewards teach the specific gamed behavior in-distribution, and how strong this is depends on monitor recall.

fits_no_version.finding: Recontextualization (generate with a misbehavior-discouraging prompt, train with a more permissive one) reduces in-task specification gaming, deception and sycophancy. It requires the prompt contrast, and is outperformed by standard training with a strong monitor.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Inoculation-style prompt contrasts during on-policy training reduce learning of the targeted in-distribution misbehavior.

record.problems: Most plotted numeric results are absent from the supplied text. The strong-monitor table is flattened, and its baseline entries cannot be reliably assigned. Several reported experiments use task-specific or synthetic settings; the post itself notes uncertainty about longer runs and instruction-following effects. In the weak-monitor GRPO setting, the authors later found that random recontextualization prompts could achieve comparable results because of a regularizing effect.
record.rows_left_out: No rows left out under the 60-row limit. Coherence and instruction-following results were excluded because they do not measure the claim's named misbehavior outcomes.

untested.parts: No measure of broad misalignment on unrelated questions after RL; only in-task hacking, deception and sycophancy.
Neither inoculation nor benign retraining is evaluated against emergent broad misalignment.

record.verdict_notes: The rows' state judgments are fine in themselves, but the record links them to V4 and V6 when they measure in-distribution target misbehavior rather than emergent broad misalignment. The weak-detector GRPO results are confounded by an importance-ratio artifact; random recontextualization prompts gave comparable results.

versions.untested_parts: No insecure-code fine-tune or matched secure-code and class-request controls.
Does not test the listed narrow fine-tunes as a source of broad misalignment on unrelated prompts.
Tests RL-associated deception and task-specific specification gaming, but not broad misaligned free-form answers on unrelated prompts or number-sequence fine-tuning.
No shared linear direction or persona-feature mediation test.
Tests recontextualization through prompt changes, not brief benign retraining.
Does not report an open-model size sweep, seed robustness and coherence-filter analysis of the claimed broad-misalignment effect, or its emergence over training in that setting.
